strengths: The paper clearly frames and formalizes the problem: the three diagnostic metrics (reward noise rate rho_noise, self-feedback bias rho_selfbias, symmetry bias rho_symbias) give a structured vocabulary for analyzing why self-rewarding RL (RLIR) lags behind RLVR, and this decomposition is a genuinely useful contribution to understanding self-rewarding dynamics.

The controlled 'decoupling experiment' (Section 3.5) is a thoughtful design: by injecting symmetric noise, asymmetric flipping, and prediction coupling into oracle rewards, the authors can isolate the causal effect of each bias type on training stability and convergence, which strengthens the empirical claims beyond mere correlation.

The proposed method (RLER) is well-motivated by the diagnostics: ensemble self-rewarding to weaken policy-reward coupling, adaptive hard/soft reward interpolation grounded in Theorem 1, and confidence-disagreement rollout selection to suppress over-reward. Each component maps to a specific diagnosed failure mode.

Ablations are fairly thorough: the component-wise ablations (Figure 5, Table 3), the interpolation variant analysis (Int v1/v2/v3), and the rollout selection analysis (Figure 6) support the necessity of each design choice, and the metrics rho_noise/rho_selfbias/rho_symbias are tracked during training for RLER versus baselines.

The paper addresses data contamination concerns with a synthetic arithmetic dataset, includes scaling experiments on unlabeled data (Figure 7), and the ensemble-to-single consolidation via model merging demonstrates practical deployability.
The writing is generally clear, and the ethics statement and hyperparameter details (Appendix B, C) support reasonable reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is limited: all experiments use the Qwen2.5 family only (1.5B for the diagnostic study, 7B for the main results), and tasks are exclusively arithmetic/math. There is no evidence the system-bias diagnosis or RLER generalizes to other domains or model families, which weakens the central claims about RLIR in general.

No statistical rigor: results appear to come from single training runs with no error bars, seeds, or significance testing. Several key comparisons are close (e.g., RLER 37.5 vs RLVR 38.9; RLER 12.1 vs Self-Consistency 13.8 on AIME25, where RLER actually loses), so run-to-run variance could materially change conclusions.

Baselines are comparatively weak and incomplete: the paper cites several more recent RLIR methods (entropy-based, Intuitor-style, TTRL variants, Co-reward) in related work but evaluates only Self-Consistency, Frequency-Based, and LLM-as-a-Judge. Comparison against stronger recent intrinsic-reward methods is needed to substantiate the +13.6% claim.

Theoretical support is thin and partly questionable. The claim MSE(r) = 2(1 - rho(r, r*)) in the Appendix A proof implicitly assumes the oracle advantage A* has unit variance standardized with the same group statistics, which does not obviously hold; Theorem 1's condition (a >= s_max, i.e., true-label probability dominates the largest tail label) is restrictive and the 'why ensemble first' convexity argument is heuristic rather than rigorous.

The rho_symbias definition (BRIR - BRsym) is ad hoc: it depends on oracle accuracy, mixes per-instance ratios with population quantities, and the presentation of Finding 2 (sign conventions of over- vs under-reward and how rho_symbias increases) is confusing and hard to follow.

Compute fairness of the ensemble is not fully convincing: even with per-policy rollouts matched (G/k = 8), RLER requires K forward/generation passes from distinct models plus a merging stage; the extra overhead relative to single-model RLIR baselines is not quantified, and the k=2 default makes the ensemble advantage hard to disentangle from effective ensemble-of-checkpoints effects.

Presentation issues: several figures (Figures 2, 3, 4) are dense, small, and difficult to read; there are grammatical errors and imprecise statements (e.g., 'greatly optimize rho_noise...'), and no code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the full pipeline.

The improvement over the best baseline is reported as +13.6%, but given RLER falls below Self-Consistency on at least one benchmark and the merged model's behavior is only briefly characterized, the strength and consistency of the headline claim deserve more careful qualification.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: why self-rewarding/intrinsic-reward RL (RLIR) lags behind RLVR, and how to diagnose the failure mode. The framing of 'system bias' via three measurable quantities (reward noise rate, self-feedback bias rate, symmetry bias rate) is a reasonable analytical lens.

The controlled decoupling experiment (Section 3.5) on a synthetic, contamination-free arithmetic dataset is a good experimental design choice: it isolates the effect of each bias type on training dynamics, and the findings (over-reward more harmful than under-reward; high-confidence errors amplified by policy–reward coupling) are plausible and useful.
Theorem 1 gives a clean (if narrow) characterization of when soft rewards dominate hard rewards under mispredicted labels, with a complete proof in the appendix.

The ablation study is fairly thorough: each component of RLER (ensemble, interpolation variants, rollout selection, model merging) is ablated, and the rollout-selection analysis in Figure 6 conditions on predicted-label correctness, which directly connects behavior to the proposed metrics.
Reproducibility of the setup is adequate: framework (Open-R1), hyperparameters, prompt templates, and hardware are reported, and a synthetic dataset is described in enough detail to reconstruct.
weaknesses: Limited evidential strength for the central claims. All headline results come from a single model family (Qwen2.5) and very small, high-variance benchmarks (AIME24/25 have ~30 problems; Avg@8 on such sets is extremely noisy). There are no error bars, no multiple seeds, and no significance testing, so differences like RLER 37.5 vs. RLVR 38.9 or HMMT24 9.6 vs. 7.9 are hard to interpret. The '+13.6% over the best baseline' figure is a relative number on small averages; the absolute gap over Self-Consistency is ~4.5 points, and RLER actually loses to SC on AIME25 (12.1 vs. 13.8).

Several of the proposed metrics are close to tautological. For SC and Frequency-based rewards, r̃i = ri by construction, so ρselfbias ≡ 1 is guaranteed rather than discovered; 'Findings' built on this (e.g., 'SC and Frequency yield ρselfbias ≡ 1') restate definitions. Similarly, ρnoise and ρsymbias require oracle rewards (ground-truth labels) to compute, which sits awkwardly with the paper's motivating claim of label-free scaling: the diagnostic framework presupposes labels that RLIR is supposed to remove.

The method itself is a relatively straightforward combination of existing techniques — ensembling self-consistency, hard/soft reward interpolation, rollout filtering, and TIES model merging. The component-wise novelty is modest, and the main intellectual contribution rests on the diagnostic analysis, which (per the previous point) is partly definitional.

Theoretical support is thin relative to the claims. Theorem 1 covers only the m ≠ t case of one hard-vs-soft comparison under idealized answer probabilities; there is no theory connecting ρsymbias or ρselfbias to convergence or stability, so the causal narratives in Findings 2–4 rest on single-configuration empirical plots.

Compute fairness is questionable. RLER trains an ensemble (k=2 sub-policies) with merged rollouts; although per-policy rollouts are halved (Gk=8), the total sampling, memory, and coordination costs differ from single-policy baselines, and there is no compute-matched comparison (e.g., a single model trained with 2× rollouts or with majority voting over a larger group, which is essentially the TTRL-style baseline and is cited but not directly compared).

The scaling claim (Section 5.4, Figure 7) is under-supported: only one figure, no variance, no details on the 8k→1024k regime (e.g., whether the ensemble is rebuilt, total compute at each size), and 'stably scalable' is asserted from a single curve.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places: Figure 5 is dense and hard to parse; several figures are low-resolution; there are grammatical errors ('a accurate and robust', 'greatly optimize ρnoise…'), an inconsistent baseline name ('RLSR'), and inconsistent notation between the metric definitions and their use. There is also no limitations section despite clear limitations (single family, oracle-dependent metrics, ensemble cost) that the authors should have discussed.

Missing comparisons with directly relevant concurrent intrinsic-reward methods (e.g., the cited TTRL, Co-Reward, or entropy-based approaches) beyond the three in-house RLIR baselines weakens the positioning of the claimed state-of-the-art improvement.

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a relevant and timely problem: why RLIR/self-rewarding RL underperforms RLVR, attributing it to system bias in self-estimated rewards. The three diagnostic metrics (ρ_noise, ρ_selfbias, ρ_symbias) provide a concrete vocabulary for analyzing reward-estimation bias, which is a genuinely useful contribution to understanding RLIR failure modes.

The controlled 'decoupling experiment' on a synthetic arithmetic dataset (with injected symmetric noise, asymmetric flipping, and prediction coupling) is a well-designed methodology for isolating the causal effect of each bias type on training dynamics, avoiding contamination issues.
Theorem 1 (hard vs. soft rewards under m ≠ t) is backed by a full derivation in Appendix A, including both sufficiency and necessity directions, connecting the analysis to concrete design choices.

RLER is well-motivated: each component (ensemble self-rewarding, adaptive soft-reward interpolation, confidence-disagreement rollout selection) is explicitly tied to one of the three diagnostic desiderata (accuracy, unbiasedness, robustness), and the component-wise ablations (Fig. 5, Table 3) largely support these attributions.

Reasonably comprehensive evaluation: two training corpora, six reasoning benchmarks, both Avg@k and Pass@k, a data-scaling study up to 1024k, and an ensemble-to-single model merging step that addresses practical deployability. Training-time metric curves (Fig. 4) connect the method back to the diagnostic framework.
The compute-matched design (per-policy rollouts G/k with k ensemble members) is a thoughtful attempt at fair comparison against single-model baselines.
weaknesses: No variance reporting: results appear to come from a single seed, yet RL training (especially self-rewarding RL, which the paper itself shows is unstable) has high run-to-run variance. The +13.6% headline improvement over the best RLIR baseline and the 'stable scaling' claim in Fig. 7 (where the SC baseline collapses toward zero at larger data sizes, which looks suspicious) would be considerably more convincing with multiple seeds and error bars.

Baseline tuning and strength are questionable. LLM-as-a-Judge degrades from 12.5 (w/o RL) to 3.3 on the benchmark suite, suggesting the baseline may be misconfigured rather than inherently weak. Comparisons against stronger/recent RLIR methods (e.g., TTRL variants, Co-reward, entropy/Intuitor-style methods cited in related work) are missing; only SC, Freq, and Judge are evaluated.

Notation and definitions in Section 3.3 are unclear: r̃_i (the self-estimated reward used in ρ_selfbias) is introduced without definition, and the claim that SC and Freq yield ρ_selfbias ≡ 1 is confusing given the stated formula. The ρ_symbias definition (a difference of balance ratios that can be negative) also lacks discussion of how to interpret its sign and scale.

The theoretical analysis is narrow: Theorem 1 covers only the m ≠ t case under a specific condition (a ≥ s_max) and relies on population-level label probabilities approximated by empirical frequencies; it does not cover the majority-correct case that dominates most of training. The empirical findings are described correlationally rather than with formal support.

RLER adds meaningful complexity: K ensemble members require additional rollout computation and memory, and the method introduces many hyperparameters (interpolation variants v1–v3, sharding strategy, selection quotas n_y, merging constants k=0.7, α=0.5). While ablations exist, the practical compute-vs-gain trade-off relative to simply running RLVR or larger-G single-model RLIR is not analyzed.

The claimed '3.6% below RLVR' gap uses relative percentages that flatter the comparison; on absolute terms, RLER (37.5) vs RLVR (38.9) is a modest gap, but on some benchmarks (AIME24: 23.3 vs 32.1; AIME25: 12.1 vs 12.5) the gap is uneven and not discussed.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: several figures are small and hard to read (Fig. 2, 3, 4 legends and axes), 'AMC24' is used as a benchmark without citation, and there are editing lapses ('greatly optimize', 'Aadvantage', inconsistent naming RLSR/RLIR). The rollout selection budget mechanism (per-answer quotas n_y) is under-specified in the main text.

No explicit limitations section; for example, the restriction to verifiable/math domains (where answer-label matching makes self-verification tractable), the sensitivity of α(x) estimation, and the applicability to non-MAP-able answer spaces are not discussed.

strengths: The paper provides a genuine diagnostic contribution: it decomposes the failure of self-rewarding RL (RLIR) into three measurable quantities (reward noise ρ_noise, policy–reward coupling ρ_selfbias, over/under-reward skew ρ_symbias) and validates each factor's role via a controlled decoupling experiment on a decontaminated synthetic arithmetic corpus, which cleanly avoids the contamination confounds that plague RLVR/RLIR comparisons.

The FP/FN correction study in Appendix B.4 is particularly convincing: partially correcting false-positive rewards yields much larger gains than fully correcting false negatives, providing direct empirical support for the central claim that over-reward drift is the primary bottleneck of RLIR.

The proposed RLER is well-motivated by the diagnosis: ensemble-based unified rewarding, adaptive soft/hard reward interpolation with a query-dependent gate α(x), and disagreement-aware rollout selection each map to one of the three diagnosed desiderata, and the component-wise ablations (Table 5, Fig. 5, Table 10) show cumulative contributions rather than a single load-bearing trick.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: multiple backbones (Qwen2.5 series, Llama 3.x) and datasets (arithmetic, DAPO-MATH-17K, BigMath, WebInstruct-verified/MMLU-Pro), comparison against recent strong RLIR baselines (INTUITOR, Co-rewarding), matched rollout budgets (K=2, Gk=8 with G_total=16), a compute-proxy analysis (Table 12) showing RLER is actually FLOPs-cheaper than single-model RLIR, hyperparameter sensitivity studies (Tables 8, 9), ensemble-size scaling (Table 13), and a random-reward control to rule out hidden data leakage.
Deployment practicality is addressed via TIES-merging to a single model with no inference overhead, and the merged model retains comparable or better accuracy (Fig. 7, Table 13).
Reproducibility support is good: full algorithm pseudocode, training hyperparameters, prompt templates, and hardware details are provided.
weaknesses: The diagnostic metrics are defined somewhat ad hoc and their interpretive validity is not fully established. In particular, ρ_selfbias = 1 − (1/G)Σ|r_i − r̃_i| is a somewhat opaque coupling measure; the claim that it captures 'how tightly bias is reinforced by the loop' is asserted rather than grounded in a formal model of the feedback dynamics. Similarly, the symmetric-noise baseline BR_sym = p_t/(1−p_t) behind ρ_symbias embeds an independence assumption that is itself the thing under dispute.

The 'ensemble' is weaker than the framing suggests: K=2 sub-policies initialized from the same backbone and trained with data sharding. With pooled rollouts, the ensemble majority m_EC over 16 pooled rollouts is essentially identical to Self-Consistency with G=16 under a matched budget, so the headline 'ensemble breaks the self-confirming loop' narrative risks overstating the architectural novelty; the actual gains appear to come substantially from the interpolation and rollout-selection machinery, as the ablations themselves show.

Margins over the strongest baseline are modest and inconsistent across benchmarks: on DAPO-MATH-17K, RLER (37.5 Avg@8) beats Co-rewarding (35.3) by +2.2, not the advertised +6.2 (which appears to come from averaging in weaker baselines), and RLER actually trails Co-rewarding on HMMT24 (9.6 vs 11.3) and AIME24 is tied. On MMLU-Pro the gap over Co-rewarding is +0.3. No error bars or multi-seed variance are reported for the main Table 1.

The controlled decoupling experiments are confined to one synthetic arithmetic task with a 1.5B model; the finding that over-reward is more harmful than under-reward may be setting-dependent (e.g., group-normalized advantages, curriculum difficulty), and its generality is assumed rather than demonstrated.

The theoretical result (Appendix C) is narrow: a condition under which Frequency rewards beat SC rewards under misalignment. It supports the soft-vs-hard trade-off discussion but does not formally analyze the self-confirming loop dynamics that motivate the paper.

The Judge baseline performs strikingly poorly (13.4 Avg@8 on DAPO-MATH-17K vs 33.0 for SC), raising implementation concerns; while Judge is not the paper's main comparison, a mis-implemented baseline inflates the apparent breadth of RLIR failure modes.

The deployment story (single merged model) is somewhat orthogonal to the bias diagnosis; merging is applied post hoc and the paper does not analyze whether the merged model inherits or reintroduces the diagnosed couplings.

strengths: The paper asks a timely and well-motivated question: why self-rewarding RL (RLIR) underperforms RLVR, and frames the answer via a 'self-confirming loop' of confidence-coupled reward bias.

The controlled decoupling experiment (synthetic reward injection isolating ρnoise, ρsymbias, ρselfbias) is a nice diagnostic design, and Appendix B.4's FP/FN correction study gives concrete evidence that over-reward (FP) noise is the primary bottleneck.

Experiments are broad: multiple backbones (Qwen2.5, Llama), datasets (DAPO-MATH-17K, BIGMATH, WebInstruct), recent RLIR baselines (INTUITOR, Co-rewarding), plus component ablations, ensemble-size scaling, hyperparameter sensitivity, and a compute-cost analysis.
The proposed method is deployed as a single merged model (TIES-Merging), so the ensemble does not increase inference cost, and the rollout budget is kept matched to single-model RLIR.
weaknesses: The central diagnostic metrics require oracle ground-truth labels to compute (ρnoise, ρsymbias are deviations from r*, and ρselfbias depends on r*). This undermines the paper's own motivating narrative: in the truly unlabeled settings RLIR targets, none of the three metrics can be measured, so the 'desiderata' cannot be checked in practice. The paper does not acknowledge this limitation.

The methodology is a stack of heuristics (ensemble averaging, token-level confidence, batch-wise quantile normalization, calibrated mass reweighting, adaptive α interpolation, disagreement-aware quotas, data sharding, TIES merging). Each component is plausible, but the paper provides no principled justification tying the specific design to the diagnosed bias mechanism, and the ablations do not disentangle why the specific choices (e.g., the weights w in §4.3) are correct rather than arbitrary.

The ρselfbias metric (Eq. 5) is defined as 1 − mean|ri − r̃i|, which is a similarity, not a 'bias rate'; its interpretation as coupling strength is never formally grounded, and the decomposition into ρtrue/ρerr adds further ad-hoc structure. The formal analysis (Appendix C) covers only the narrow case of Freq vs. SC under m ≠ t with a second-largest-mass condition; the theory is thin relative to the breadth of claims.

Gains over the strongest baseline are modest and possibly within run-to-run variance: RLER 37.5 vs. Co-rewarding 35.3 Avg@8 on the main benchmark (a 2.2-point gap), and no error bars, seeds, or variance estimates are reported for the main tables, making the headline +6.2% claim hard to assess. The Judge baseline's near-collapse (13.4) also raises implementation/fairness questions.

The ensemble requires loading K=2+ models in parallel during training (~2–8× VRAM per the paper's own analysis), a real practical cost for the resource-constrained unlabeled-RL scenarios the paper targets; the compute proxy excludes this memory bottleneck.

Several key results are only visible in small, hard-to-read figures (Figs. 2, 3, 5), the text contains typos and imprecision ('a accurate', inconsistent 'Findings' numbering), there is no explicit limitations section, and no code release is mentioned, weakening reproducibility.

The synthetic arithmetic testbed used for diagnosis involves injected, exogenously controlled noise, which differs qualitatively from the endogenous, non-stationary noise of actual RLIR; the transfer of the decoupling findings to real RLIR dynamics is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated diagnostic framework: the three metrics (reward noise rate, policy-reward coupling, over/under-reward skew) decompose the self-confirming loop phenomenon in a way that is intuitive and empirically tractable.

The controlled decoupling experiment (Section 3.5, synthetic reward injection on an arithmetic testbed) is a genuinely valuable analysis that isolates each bias factor's effect on RLIR training dynamics, supporting the causal claims about noise, coupling, and over-reward skew rather than only observing correlations.

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple backbones (Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B), multiple datasets (DAPO-MATH-17K, BIGMATH, WebInstruct-verified, MMLU-PRO), strong recent baselines (INTUITOR, Co-rewarding), and an honest RLVR upper bound comparison.

Thorough component ablations (Figure 5, Tables 5, 10) that trace each mechanism's contribution, plus the fixed-vs-adaptive interpolation comparison showing gains come from the query-dependent gate rather than interpolation per se.

Practical attention to deployment: ensemble-to-single consolidation via TIES-Merging, compute/memory analysis (Tables 12-13), a clear justification for the k=2 default, and hyperparameter robustness studies (temperature, interpolation bounds).

Useful supporting evidence for the FP-dominance claim (Appendix B.4 FP/FN correction study) and a decontaminated synthetic dataset with a random-reward control that rules out memorization as an alternative explanation.

Includes a small theory section (Appendix C) with a clean necessary-and-sufficient condition for when soft rewards beat hard rewards under misalignment, plus a proof sketch of the correctness-confidence effect.
weaknesses: Gain over the strongest baseline is modest on the main benchmark: RLER improves Avg@8 by 2.2 points over Co-rewarding (37.5 vs 35.3) and trails RLVR by 1.4; on HMMT24 RLER (9.6) is below Co-rewarding (11.3). No seed variance or statistical significance is reported for the main Table 1 results, so the central claim rests on single-run numbers.

The diagnostic metrics require ground-truth labels to compute, which is only available in verifiable domains; the paper's broader motivation (private corpora, unlabeled industrial data) cannot be validated with these metrics, and the WebInstruct extension relies on an external LLM verifier, blurring the line between intrinsic and extrinsic rewards.

The ensemble requirement doubles (or multiplies) VRAM during training and the paper's answer to diversity is data sharding alone; all sub-policies start from the same initialization, so the claimed decorrelation depends on one training regime and its generality beyond math reasoning is untested.

The diagnosis-to-method link is partly post-hoc: RLER has many interacting components (ensemble aggregation, calibrated mass, min-max normalization, adaptive gate, disagreement-aware selection, budget caps), and while ablations show each helps, the principled mapping from the three desiderata to these specific design choices could be tightened.

Theory covers only a narrow special case (soft vs. hard reward under m != t with the second-largest-mass condition); the theoretical analysis does not characterize when ensembling helps, which is the core of the method.

Presentation has rough edges: several typos and minor inconsistencies (e.g., 'a accurate' in Section 4.2, duplicated Figure 8 caption text in Appendix B.1.1, references to 'Table B.2.1' whose labeling is confusing), and Figure 2's decoupling plots are hard to read at the printed scale.

The stable-scaling claim (Figure 7) is evaluated at training-set sizes up to 1M but details of how the scaling comparison was run (e.g., fixed step budget vs. fixed epochs) are sparse, and only the SC baseline is shown as the RLIR comparator in that figure.
